title: Which application segment a destination maps to when several overlap
aliases: traffic goes direct instead of through zpa
specific fqdn segment removes host from wildcard
no match in this application segment
works by hostname but not by ip
raw ip not going through zpa

prose.text: This subject covers how a destination is mapped to one application segment when several overlap.

prose.label: Selection.
prose.text: Exact match is the default, and it attempts the more granular segment: [[zpa.policy.multimatch:exact-match-default]]. {{granularity-ranking}} Ties and the part port ranges play are open {{gap:same-specificity-tie}} {{gap:granularity-port-narrowness}}.

prose.label: When the port is not listed.
prose.text: {{port-mismatch-bypass}} {{example-no-fallback}} The client drops the access and sends nothing to the cloud: [[zpa.policy.multimatch:port-mismatch-dropped]]. The sources word the outcome two ways {{divergence:bypass-or-drop}}, and what happens to the bypassed traffic is open {{gap:post-bypass-outcome}}.

prose.label: Carve-outs.
prose.text: A specific FQDN is removed from the wildcard segment by default: [[zpa.policy.multimatch:carved-out-by-default]]. {{carve-out-ip}} {{wildcard-dead-for-carved-ports}} {{fix-for-carve-out}} What Multimatch changes is in [[zpa.app-segments.multimatch]].

prose.label: What outranks granularity.
prose.text: The Bypass setting is covered in [[zpa.app-segments.bypass]]. Access policy runs on the chosen segment: [[zpa.policy.evaluation-order]]. The access log schema for checking which segment matched is [[zpa.logs.user-activity]].

checks.do: Whether the destination port is listed on the most granular segment that covers the host, since a miss there ends in a client-side bypass and never reaches a wider segment.
Whether a specific-FQDN or /32 segment exists for the host, because it removes the host from the wildcard or subnet segment for every port it does not list.
Whether the request appears in Private Access diagnostics at all; a port mismatch never reaches the cloud, so absence there points at segment selection.
Whether two overlapping segments are equally granular, which no source ranks.

granularity-ranking.statement: Granularity is judged on the domain or address: an exact host is more specific than a wildcard that contains it, and for IPs a /32 host is more specific than the /24 that contains it.
granularity-ranking.conditions: Chain of evidence: no source defines 'more granular' in words. The ranking is read from the order of the documented Multimatch examples, which list matches 'from most specific to least specific', and from the /32 versus /24 carve-out example. Corrected on recapture (2026-10-18): previously "Granularity is judged on the domain or address: an exact host is more specific than a wildcard that contains it, and a longer wildcard suffix is more specific than a shorter one (`server1.db.hr.company.com`, then `*.db.hr.company.com`, `*.hr.company.com`, `*.company.com`, `*.com`); for IPs a /32 host is more specific than the /24 that contains it.". The wildcard-suffix ordering (server1.db.hr.company.com, then *.db.hr.company.com, *.hr.company.com, *.company.com, *.com) was read from the Multimatch example table, which the recapture no longer carries; that clause is removed.

quotes: Multiple matches apply to applications from most specific to least specific.
the destination address maps to the more specific application segment, which is Server1_AS.
because the moment the IP address is created, the 10.0.0.1/32 host is carved out of Subnet_AS 10.0.0.0/24.

port-mismatch-bypass.statement: If there is no match in the more granular application segment for the destination port, Zscaler Client Connector bypasses Private Access and sends the traffic directly.

quotes: If there is no match in this application segment for the destination port, Zscaler Client Connector bypasses Private Access (ZPA) and sends traffic directly.
If two or more application segments cover the same destination address, Zscaler Client Connector attempts to match traffic to the more granular application segment.

example-no-fallback.statement: In the documented example, Segment 1 is `*.example.com` on TCP and UDP 1-65535 and Segment 2 is `www.example.com` on TCP 8843; a request to `www.example.com:80` resolves to Segment 2, fails at the closed port, and is not forwarded to Segment 1.

quotes: If a user navigates to www.example.com:80, the request resolves to the more specific FQDN in Application Segment 2, but fails at the closed port 80. Zscaler Client Connector does not forward traffic to Application Segment 1
Application Segment 1 - FQDN: *.example.com - Ports: TCP 1-65535 UDP 1-65535 - Application Segment 2 - FQDN: www.example.com - Ports: TCP 8843

carve-out-ip.statement: The same carve-out applies to IP addresses: the moment an application segment is created for 10.0.0.1/32, that host is carved out of the segment for 10.0.0.0/24.

quotes: because the moment the IP address is created, the 10.0.0.1/32 host is carved out of Subnet_AS 10.0.0.0/24.
Even with an IP address, the default behavior of Private Access is to perform an exact match of applications.

wildcard-dead-for-carved-ports.statement: Without Multimatch, a wildcard segment never receives a request for a host that has its own segment on any port that segment does not list; the request is not forwarded to the wildcard segment.
wildcard-dead-for-carved-ports.conditions: Chain of evidence: the carve-out removes the host from the wildcard segment, and a port miss in the host's own segment ends in a client-side bypass with no fallback. Statement changed after verification: 'is bypassed at the client' replaced by 'is not forwarded to the wildcard segment', since bypass versus drop is open (divergence bypass-or-drop).

fix-for-carve-out.statement: The documented fixes for a carved-out host are to configure the missing port on the specific segment, or to enable Multimatch, which makes the wildcard segment catch ports the specific segment does not define.

quotes: To fix this, TCP port 3389 must be configured for the Server1_AS application segment, or Multimatch can be enabled.
Enabling Multimatch changes the behavior of the wildcard application segment, and catches access to ports that have not been defined in the more specific FQDN application segment.

raw-ip-no-dns-interception.statement: A connection made to a raw IP address sends no DNS request, so Client Connector's DNS interception never hands it a synthetic address: a segment defined only by FQDN does not capture it, and Private Access carries it only if an IP-based segment covers that address.
raw-ip-no-dns-interception.conditions: Inferred from the help's description of interception, which starts from the client's DNS request for a protected domain; no captured source states the raw-IP case. Confirm with a lab test: an FQDN-only segment, then connect to the server's IP.

bypass-or-drop.summary: The same Understanding Application Access passage describes a port mismatch as a client-side bypass to direct traffic and as a drop by Private Access.

quotes: If there is no match in this application segment for the destination port, Zscaler Client Connector bypasses Private Access (ZPA) and sends traffic directly.

positions.says: Zscaler Client Connector bypasses Private Access and sends the traffic directly.

quotes: Zscaler Client Connector does not forward traffic to Application Segment 1, and the client connection request is dropped by Private Access.

positions.says: The client connection request is dropped by Private Access.

bypass-or-drop.impact: An answer that says the request reaches the destination directly, or that it fails, goes beyond what the passage establishes; both wordings agree that the request is not forwarded to Private Access.

same-specificity-tie.title: Which segment is used when overlapping segments are equally granular, or share the same FQDN and the same Bypass setting
same-specificity-tie.blocks: deterministic answers for two segments with identical domain names, or two segments for one FQDN that both set Bypass to Always or both to On Corporate Network
same-specificity-tie.detail: No captured source states a tie-break. Unverified legacy statements: save-time validation likely blocks two EXCLUSIVE segments with identical FQDNs (only the mixed Multimatch setting conflict is documented); if both were saved, Zscaler Client Connector picks one deterministically per session and which one is unspecified. Test in a scratch tenant with two segments with identical domain_names and match_style, then inspect the access logs for the matched segment.

granularity-port-narrowness.title: Whether port-range narrowness plays any part in 'more granular'
granularity-port-narrowness.blocks: ranking two segments that cover the same host with different port sets
granularity-port-narrowness.detail: Unverified legacy statement: 'port-range narrowness does not enter the granularity judgment' (stated in the resolved ledger answer for zpa-02). No captured source says it; the documented examples only vary the domain. Test with two segments for one host that differ only in port ranges.

post-bypass-outcome.title: What happens to traffic after Zscaler Client Connector bypasses Private Access on a port mismatch
post-bypass-outcome.blocks: saying whether a bypassed request reaches the destination, is blocked elsewhere, or never resolves
post-bypass-outcome.detail: Unverified legacy statement: what happens to the traffic after depends on the client's forwarding profile and network egress, outside the application segment configuration. No captured source describes the post-bypass path. Test with Zscaler Client Connector on a port-mismatch request and a packet capture on the device.
